subject: chemistry
title: Alkenes and electrophilic addition
key_idea: **Alkenes** are unsaturated hydrocarbons with a C=C double bond, made of a σ bond and a weaker π bond. The π bond is a region of high electron density, so alkenes are attacked by **electrophiles**. They react by electrophilic addition, and the major product follows the stability of the carbocation.

blocks.text: An alkene has at least one C=C bond. This section covers how that bond is made, its shape and why it makes alkenes reactive.

items.meaning: Containing at least one multiple carbon–carbon bond.
Formed by orbitals overlapping directly between the two atoms.
Formed by sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals, above and below the line between the two carbon atoms.

items: The general formula of an alkene is **CₙH₂ₙ**. Cycloalkenes are also unsaturated hydrocarbons.
The C=C bond is one **σ bond** and one **π bond**.
The π bond cannot rotate, so rotation about the C=C is restricted.
Each carbon of the C=C has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so the shape around it is **trigonal planar**.
The bond angle is **120°**.
The π bond has a **low bond enthalpy**, so it breaks more easily than a σ bond.
The π bond is a centre of **high electron density**, which attracts electrophiles.
A reaction breaks the π bond and makes two new σ bonds.
C=C is a σ bond plus a π bond. The shape around each carbon is trigonal planar, with 120° bond angles.
The π bond is weaker and electron-rich, so alkenes react by addition.

blocks.text: Alkenes react by addition, where the C=C bond opens and two new atoms or groups join. The reagents and products are below.

items: Hydrogenation of unsaturated vegetable oils with a nickel catalyst makes margarine.
In hydrogenation, the alkene turns into an alkane: C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆.
In the manganate(VII) reaction, the purple solution turns colourless as the double bond is oxidised to a diol.
Shake the compound with **bromine water**, or add bromine.
An alkene turns the orange or brown solution **colourless**, because the bromine adds across the C=C.
An alkane does not decolourise bromine water in the dark.
Alkenes add H₂, halogens, hydrogen halides and steam across the C=C bond.
Bromine water going from orange to colourless is the test for unsaturation.

blocks.text: An electrophile is attracted to the π bond. The reaction goes in two steps through a carbocation intermediate.

items.meaning: An ion with a positively charged carbon atom, formed as an intermediate.

items.text: HBr is already polar, with δ+ on hydrogen. Br₂ is non-polar, but the π electrons of the C=C repel its bonding pair and polarise it.
A curly arrow from the C=C bond goes to the δ+ hydrogen, and a curly arrow from the H–Br bond goes to the bromine.
This gives a carbocation and a Br⁻ ion.
A curly arrow from a lone pair on Br⁻ goes to the positive carbon, which makes the C–Br bond.

items: Curly arrows start from a **bond** or a **lone pair**, never from an atom.
In the reaction with a halogen, the intermediate may be drawn as a carbocation or as a halonium ion.
The bond breaks heterolytically, because Br⁻ takes both electrons of the H–Br bond.
The electrophile is attracted to the C=C. The first step makes a carbocation, and the second step adds the negative ion.
Curly arrows begin at a bond or a lone pair.

blocks.text: When HBr adds to an unsymmetrical alkene such as propene, two products are possible. One is formed in greater amount.

items: The H⁺ can add to either carbon of the C=C, giving a **primary** or a **secondary** carbocation.
Alkyl groups push electron density towards the positive carbon, which stabilises it. This is the **inductive effect**.
Stability increases in the order **primary < secondary < tertiary**.
The more stable carbocation forms more easily and in greater amount, so it leads to the **major product**.
Propene + HBr: the secondary carbocation gives **2-bromopropane** as the major product.
The primary carbocation gives 1-bromopropane as the minor product.
Markovnikov's rule: the hydrogen adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens, so the halogen ends up on the more substituted carbon.

diagram.alt: A predictor: pick an alkene and see the major product when it reacts with hydrogen bromide.
diagram.prompt: Pick an alkene that reacts with HBr

options.label: Ethene
options.explanation: Ethene is symmetrical, so both carbons give the same primary carbocation.

options.label: Propene
options.explanation: H adds to the CH₂ carbon, leaving the positive charge on the middle carbon.

options.label: But-1-ene
options.explanation: The positive charge sits on carbon 2, which has two alkyl groups attached.

options.label: 2-methylpropene
options.explanation: The positive charge sits on the carbon with three alkyl groups, which is the most stable carbocation.

items: Carbocation stability rises from primary to secondary to tertiary.
The more stable carbocation gives the major product.

checks.q: Describe what you would see when ethene is shaken with bromine water, and explain the result.
checks.a: The orange bromine water turns colourless. Bromine adds across the C=C double bond, so it is no longer present as Br₂.

checks.q: Outline the mechanism for the addition of HBr to ethene.
checks.a: The C=C π bond attacks the δ+ H of H–Br. The H–Br bond breaks heterolytically and both electrons go to Br, giving Br⁻. A carbocation CH₃CH₂⁺ forms. A lone pair on Br⁻ attacks the positive carbon to make CH₃CH₂Br.

checks.q: Explain why the main product of the reaction of HBr with propene is 2-bromopropane.
checks.a: The intermediate carbocation can be primary or secondary. Alkyl groups donate electron density by the inductive effect, so the secondary carbocation is more stable. It forms more readily, so 2-bromopropane is the major product.

items: Hybridisation is not required.
The reactivity of alkenes is explained by the relatively low bond enthalpy of the π bond.
Know the term electrophile: an electron pair acceptor.
The rule used for the major product is Markownikoff's rule, in terms of carbocation stability. Limited to primary, secondary and tertiary. Explaining why they differ in stability is not required.
Margarine manufacture by catalytic hydrogenation of unsaturated vegetable oils is expected.
Oxidation by acidified potassium manganate(VII) gives a diol.
Give mechanisms with curly arrows for halogens and hydrogen halides, and for other binary compounds that are given.
Know the relative stability of primary, secondary and tertiary carbocations.
Know the bromine or bromine water test for a C=C bond.
Know the mechanisms for the reactions of alkenes with HBr, H₂SO₄ and Br₂.
The reaction with H₂SO₄ gives an alkyl hydrogensulfate, such as CH₃CH₂OSO₂OH from ethene.
Water then hydrolyses the hydrogensulfate to an alcohol.
Explain major and minor products by the relative stability of primary, secondary and tertiary carbocations.
Recall how alkenes are made: elimination of HX from a halogenoalkane with ethanolic NaOH and heat, dehydration of an alcohol with heated Al₂O₃ or concentrated H₂SO₄, and cracking of a longer alkane.
Hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO₄ cleaves the C=C. The products show where the double bond was in a larger molecule.
Use bromine/ethene and hydrogen bromide/propene as the mechanism examples.
Use aqueous bromine to show a C=C bond.
In addition polymerisation, many alkene molecules join with no other product. Ethene gives poly(ethene), repeat unit –CH₂–CH₂–, and propene gives poly(propene), repeat unit –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–.
